questions.question: Why does RNTL's `fireEvent.press` play the same role as `userEvent.click` on the web?
options: They are unrelated APIs with no shared purpose
Both simulate a real user interaction (a touch vs a click) on an element, driving the test from the user's perspective rather than calling internal handlers directly
fireEvent.press only works in Detox, not Jest
press is a deprecated alias for click
questions.explanation: Both APIs exist to simulate how a real user would interact with the rendered UI, keeping the test focused on behavior rather than implementation.

questions.question: Why must a native module like AsyncStorage be mocked in Jest tests?
options: Mocking is only a style preference with no functional necessity
The real module is backed by native Swift/Kotlin code that doesn't exist in the Node.js environment Jest runs tests in, so importing it directly would crash
Jest cannot import any npm package
AsyncStorage is always synchronous in tests
questions.explanation: Native modules bridge to platform-specific code; outside a real app runtime (like Jest's Node environment), that native implementation simply isn't present, so a JS-level mock stands in for it.

questions.question: What can Detox catch that a Jest + RNTL component test cannot?
options: Nothing — they test exactly the same things
Issues that only appear on a real device/simulator, like native permission dialogs, real navigation transitions, or actual screen-size layout bugs
Whether a component re-renders too often
questions.explanation: Component tests run entirely in Node and never touch real native behavior; Detox drives an actual simulator/emulator, exercising the full native + JS stack together.

questions.question: What's the recommended balance between component tests and Detox end-to-end tests?
options: Write only Detox tests and skip component tests entirely
Many fast component tests for broad coverage, with a much smaller number of slower Detox tests reserved for critical end-to-end flows
Write only component tests; Detox is never necessary
They should always be written in a 1:1 ratio
questions.explanation: Detox tests are slower and more brittle due to real device/timing dependencies, so they're best reserved for a small set of critical flows, while component tests handle broad day-to-day coverage.
